# The Strange Comfort of Small Failures

I've been thinking about how we treat small failures like they're practice rounds for the big ones. We stumble on a word while speaking and mentally file it away—*remember that next time*. We burn toast and adjust the heat. We send an awkward text and cringe, but we survive.

What strikes me is how rarely we acknowledge that surviving these tiny disasters might actually be the whole point. We're so focused on optimization, on becoming better versions of ourselves, that we miss the quiet reassurance embedded in failure itself: *you can handle this*.

There's something almost defiant about messing up in small ways. It proves we're not machines, that we're allowed to be imperfect, that the world doesn't end when we're not at our best. And yet our culture treats mistakes like moral failures, as if stuttering during a presentation reflects something fundamental about your worth.

I wonder if we'd all be a little braver if we celebrated the small stuff more—not the failures themselves, but our resilience in the face of them. The fact that you can laugh at yourself. That you can try again.

Maybe that's what confidence actually is: not the absence of mistakes, but enough experience with small ones that you stop being shocked by your own humanity. You realize that imperfection isn't something to overcome; it's something to accept, move through, and keep going.

That feels like freedom.
